recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say what you do to 4x² − 9 before differentiating, and why that makes the second derivative shorter.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split the logarithm and differentiate once
steps.margin_note: First mark. Either route is accepted; differentiating directly gives dy/dx = 8x/(4x² − 9), which is the same thing. Domain: 4x² − 9 > 0, so x > 3/2 or x < −3/2.
steps.memory_tip: A difference of two squares inside a logarithm becomes two logarithms added. Factorise before differentiating, not after.
lines: 4x² − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3), and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
Differentiate once, using the chain rule on each term:

recall.must_convey: That 4x² − 9 is factorised and the logarithm split into log(2x − 3) + log(2x + 3), giving dy/dx = 2/(2x − 3) + 2/(2x + 3).
accept: factorise four x squared minus nine into two x minus three and two x plus three
log of a product splits into a sum of logs
the first derivative is two over two x minus three plus two over two x plus three
modata factorise chesi rendu logs ga rayali
differentiating directly gives eight x over four x squared minus nine

steps.why: Differentiating log(4x² − 9) directly gives 8x/(4x² − 9), and the second derivative then needs the quotient rule on that. Splitting first replaces one quotient rule with two simple powers. The split itself needs x > 3/2, where both factors are positive; the derivative it produces is the same one that holds on x < −3/2.
common_mistakes: Writing log(4x² − 9) as log 4x² − log 9, which is not a valid split.
Writing d/dx log(2x − 3) as 1/(2x − 3), losing the inner 2.

steps.label: Differentiate a second time
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Either form is a complete answer. Check at x = 2: −4/1 − 4/49 = −4.0816, and the numerical second derivative there is −4.0816 as well.
steps.memory_tip: Both terms have the same shape, so differentiate one and copy the pattern with the sign inside changed.
lines: Write each term as a power:  dy/dx = 2(2x − 3)⁻¹ + 2(2x + 3)⁻¹
Differentiate again by the chain rule on each:

recall.must_convey: That each term differentiates to −4 over its own square, giving y″ = −4/(2x − 3)² − 4/(2x + 3)².
accept: each term gives minus four over its square
the second derivative is minus four over two x minus three squared minus four over two x plus three squared
over a common denominator it is minus eight into four x squared plus nine over four x squared minus nine squared
rendu terms nunchi minus four ostundi
both terms are negative so the second derivative is negative

steps.why: Both terms differentiate the same way, so the second derivative comes out in a single line. Putting the two over a common denominator gives the single-fraction form, which is the same answer written differently.
common_mistakes: Writing +4/(2x − 3)² + 4/(2x + 3)², missing the minus that comes from the power −1.
Forgetting the inner 2 on each term and writing −1/(2x − 3)² − 1/(2x + 3)².

insider_note: Factorise first and split the log into a sum — differentiating log(4x² − 9) directly makes the second derivative much messier. Each piece is then a simple power.
